[BUG] `TableDataElement.on_text` clobbers syntax-highlight spans for inline code
- [x] I've checked [docs](https://rich.readthedocs.io/en/latest/introduction.html) and [closed issues](https://github.com/Textualize/rich/issues?q=is%3Aissue+is%3Aclosed) for possible solutions.
- [x] I can't find my issue in the [FAQ](https://github.com/Textualize/rich/blob/master/FAQ.md).

When using `Markdown` with `inline_code_lexer` and `inline_code_theme`, inline code (backticks) inside table cells loses its syntax highlighting and falls back to the default `markdown.code` style. The same inline code renders correctly in paragraphs, headings, and list items.

**Root cause:**

`TableDataElement.on_text` (markdown.py) unconditionally applies `context.current_style` over the text:

```python
def on_text(self, context: MarkdownContext, text: TextType) -> None:
    text = Text(text) if isinstance(text, str) else text
    text.stylize(context.current_style)
    self.content.append_text(text)
```

When `MarkdownContext.on_text` processes a `code_inline` token, it produces a `Text` object with per-character syntax-highlight spans. But `TableDataElement.on_text` then calls `text.stylize(context.current_style)` on that `Text` object, which overwrites all the highlight spans with the flat `markdown.code` style.

Compare with `TextElement.on_text`, which correctly avoids this:

```python
def on_text(self, context: MarkdownContext, text: TextType) -> None:
    self.text.append(text, context.current_style if isinstance(text, str) else None)
```

Here, the style is only applied when `text` is a plain string. When it's already a highlighted `Text` object, `None` is passed, preserving the spans.

**Fix:**

`TableDataElement.on_text` should follow the same pattern:

```python
def on_text(self, context: MarkdownContext, text: TextType) -> None:
    if isinstance(text, str):
        self.content.append(text, context.current_style)
    else:
        self.content.append_text(text)
```

**Repro:**

```python
from rich.console import Console
from rich.markdown import Markdown

md = Markdown(
    "| Col |\n|---|\n| `hello` |\n\n`hello`",
    inline_code_theme="monokai",
    inline_code_lexer="python",
)
Console().print(md)
```

The standalone `` `hello` `` renders with the monokai theme; the one inside the table does not.

[BUG] Wrong terminal size when piping to a Rich app
When using a Console between two pipes, i.e `git diff | dunk | less -R` The output width is not the full width of the terminal by default.

Inside `dunk`, it's worked around by doing `Console(force_terminal=True, width=os.get_terminal_size(2))` which results in the content that gets piped into less being the whole terminal width.

[REQUEST] Add explicit support for NamedTuples
The Pretty class doesn't support pretty printing NamedTuples.

We should attempt to auto detect named tuples in order to expand these on to multiple lines as appropriate.

NamedTuples inherit from `tuple` and don't have a common base class. They have a `_fields` attribute which could identify them as a named tuple. 

We will also need to check if a custom __repr__ has been provided (in the same was as we do dataclasses).

[BUG] Chunks of text go missing when writing Asian text (wrapping issue)
### Description

(Originally reported in Textual: https://github.com/Textualize/textual/issues/3567)

When you print Asian text (specifically Chinese and Japanese, which do not use spaces), portions of the text go missing, making it unreadable.

This seems to be related to wrapping, as the characters which go missing are at the end of a line.
Instead of being wrapped on to a new line, they disappear.

There are [rules for wrapping](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Line_breaking_rules_in_East_Asian_languages) in these languages which would take more effort to adhere to, but at the very least, text should not go missing when printed.

### Examples

For example, running the snippet below, the `7` in `1670` disappears:

```python
from rich.console import Console
console = Console(width=20)
console.print("アプリケーションは1670万色を使用でき")
```

Output:

```
アプリケーションは16
0万色を使用でき
```

And in many cases, like those reported in this issue, multiple characters disappear:

```python
from rich.console import Console
console = Console(width=20)
console.print("TextualはPythonの高速アプリケーション開発フレームワークです")
```

Output:

```
TextualはPy
thonの高速アプリ
ケーション開発フレー
```

Notice that many of the characters at the end of the text are completely missing (`ムワークです`).

To reproduce the bug: ``` from httpx import Client Client().get("https://reason.com/search/?f[author][]=nick-gillespie&q=*&s=-pubdate") ``` It would throw a ResolutionError error about the URL. Unexpected default salt in 2.0.0 where I used to pass None as a salt in 1.1.0
Hi,

Not sure if this is anything you want to fix, but I wanted to at least highlight the issue:

Calling `Serializer` in 1.1.0  with a salt set to `None` used to work fine:

```python
>>> from itsdangerous.serializer import Serializer
... s = Serializer("secret-key", salt=None)
... print(s.dumps([1, 2, 3, 4]))
[1, 2, 3, 4].d6HwOZMIWe0UH9BUzXfN7AiMWXk
```

but in version 2.0.0 this throws an exception: 

```python
>>> from itsdangerous.serializer import Serializer
... s = Serializer("secret-key", salt=None)
... print(s.dumps([1, 2, 3, 4]))
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 3, in <module>
  File ".../python3.8/site-packages/itsdangerous/serializer.py", line 203, in dumps
    rv = self.make_signer(salt).sign(payload)
  File ".../python3.8/site-packages/itsdangerous/signer.py", line 211, in sign
    return value + self.sep + self.get_signature(value)
  File ".../python3.8/site-packages/itsdangerous/signer.py", line 204, in get_signature
    key = self.derive_key()
  File ".../python3.8/site-packages/itsdangerous/signer.py", line 190, in derive_key
    bytes, self.digest_method(self.salt + b"signer" + secret_key).digest()
TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +: 'NoneType' and 'bytes'
``` 

In my code, this happens because the `Serializer` is called from another function that has a salt keyword argument that is set to `None`, something along the lines of:
```python
from itsdangerous.serializer import Serializer
def init_serializer_old(secret, salt=None):
    # do stuff
    return Serializer(secret, salt)
```

Naively I now changed the code to only pass the salt keyword argument on if it is not `None`, something along the lines of:
```python
from itsdangerous.serializer import Serializer
def init_serializer_new(secret, salt=None):
    kwargs = {}
    if salt:
        kwargs['salt'] = salt
    # do stuff
    return Serializer(secret, **kwargs)
```

Using that though, generates a different signature, than the first code snippet above:

```python
>>> s = init_serializer_new("secret-key")
... print(s.dumps([1, 2, 3, 4]))
[1, 2, 3, 4].r7R9RhGgDPvvWl3iNzLuIIfELmo
```

It turns out that this is because both `Serializer` and `Signer` provide a default value for the salt argument, `b"itsdangerous"` and `b"itsdangerous.Signer"` respectively. However in 1.1.0 `Signer` accepted `None` as a salt and if so would use the value `b"itsdangerous.Signer"`. This is no longer the case due to this change:
https://github.com/pallets/itsdangerous/commit/aed5b260111c19e91af839c2c64d771c794250a0#diff-1d0e89827237bbe1bf2e65ff4801829cb4737a4679b4f14edaddd4b0414030cdL137

If I no longer pass `None` in version 2.0.0 as the salt, the default is taken from `Serializer` and is therefore different from when I explicitly passed `None` in 1.1.0 and it was taken from `Signer`. This can be fixed in my own code fairly easily:

```python
from itsdangerous.serializer import Serializer
def init_serializer_new_v2(secret, salt=b"itsdangerous.Signer"):
    # do stuff
    return Serializer(secret, salt)
```

We caught this in our tests, but others may not be so lucky, so I at least wanted to document this new behaviour here.

Environment:

- Python version: python3.8
- ItsDangerous version: 2.0.0

TimedSerializer accepts timestamps from the future
My team too was "hit" by https://github.com/pallets/itsdangerous/issues/120 not having read the change log carefully enough.

Digging deeper, a colleague discovered that while `(signs) 0.24 -> 1.1.0 (verifies)` path is broken / requires a work-around, the `1.1.0 -> 0.24` path still kinda works.

It works by the virtue of 1.1.0 sending much larger timestamps (numerically), which are interpreted as being far in the future by 0.24. Thus true positives (recent messages) work, and false positives appear (1.1.0 outdated messages are interpreted as valid by 0.24).

This is because TimedSerializer/TimestampSigner only validate that `message more recent than X`.

I have a gut feeling that it's unsafe (although a point was made that since both sender and recipient are under control of same party, this is hard to exploit).

I think that validation should be `message in interval [now, now+max_age)`, perhaps with affordance for clock drift / imperfect time synchronisation it would be `[now - ε, now + max_age + ε)`

Consider making `Serializer` generic in `t.AnyStr` for type checking to avoid overly ambiguous return types
Currently `Serializer.dumps` has an ambiguous return type (`str | bytes`) due to how the Serializer determines its own return type in `__init__` however for some of the derived classes such as `URLSafeSerializer` we know statically that the return type will be `str` and not `bytes`.

If `Serializer` were generic we could perform this type narrowing when we inherit from `Serializer` by instead inheriting from `Serializer[str]`. That way we don't need to `type:ignore` or `assert isinstance(a, str)` everywhere we use a `URLSafeSerializer` and correctly expect to get a `str` back from `dumps`.

If you wanted to be a bit more fancy you could even define a generic Protocol for the custom serializer that's passed in `__init__` (rather than use `Any`) and create overloads to return the correct Serializer type, i.e. if `dumps` on the Serializer that's passed in returns bytes, then it will return `Serializer[bytes]`, the default with `None` can then return `Serializer[str]`.

i.e. something like this: (it would require a bit more care due to the order of arguments, to properly match every possible case, but the basic idea should come across)
```python
class Serializer(_t.Generic[_t.AnyStr]):

   @_t.overload
    def __init__(
        self: Serializer[str],
        secret_key: _t_secret_key,
        salt: _t_opt_str_bytes = ...,
        serializer: _t.Optional[_SerializerProtocol[str]] = ...,
        serializer_kwargs: _t_opt_kwargs = ...,
        signer: _t.Optional[_t_signer] = ...,
        signer_kwargs: _t_opt_kwargs = ...,
        fallback_signers: _t.Optional[_t_fallbacks] = ...,
    ): ...

   @_t.overload
    def __init__(
        self: Serializer[bytes],
        secret_key: _t_secret_key,
        salt: _t_opt_str_bytes,
        serializer: _SerializerProtocol[bytes],
        serializer_kwargs: _t_opt_kwargs = ...,
        signer: _t.Optional[_t_signer] = ...,
        signer_kwargs: _t_opt_kwargs = ...,
        fallback_signers: _t.Optional[_t_fallbacks] = ...,
    ): ...

   # fallback for when the passed in serializer can't be pattern matched
   @_t.overload
    def __init__(
        self,
        secret_key: _t_secret_key,
        salt: _t_opt_str_bytes,
        serializer: Any,
        serializer_kwargs: _t_opt_kwargs = ...,
        signer: _t.Optional[_t_signer] = ...,
        signer_kwargs: _t_opt_kwargs = ...,
        fallback_signers: _t.Optional[_t_fallbacks] = ...,
    ): ...
```

Serializer.load_payload overrides in subclasses have incompatible signatures
[Mypy](https://github.com/python/mypy) recently introduced stricter checks for function signature compatibility (https://github.com/python/mypy/pull/2521). Since `itsdangerous` is included in the typeshed library with typing stubs, it found an issue with the signatures of `load_payload`. Consider:
```py3
class Serializer:
  def load_payload(self, payload, serializer=None): ...
```
vs.
```py3
class JSONWebSignatureSerializer(Serializer):
  def load_payload(self, payload, return_header=False): ...
```
vs.
```py3
class URLSafeSerializerMixin(object):
  def load_payload(self, payload): ...

class URLSafeSerializer(URLSafeSerializerMixin, Serializer): ...
class TimedSerializer(Serializer): ...
class URLSafeTimedSerializer(URLSafeSerializerMixin, TimedSerializer): ...
```

Basically, it's invalid to replace `load_payload()` accepting an optional kwarg with an implementation that doesn't.

`Response.location` and `content_location` should use `iri_to_uri`
They currently store strings, then call `iri_to_uri` in `get_wsgi_headers`. And that's only done for WSGI, so sans-IO/ASGI doesn't get it. Instead, they should always be stored as URIs, and accessed as IRIs.

No other headers are "fixed" in `get_wsgi_headers`. `Response.headers` is considered "raw" values, where it's the responsibility of the code setting it to set a valid value. That's what the properties provide: set a Python value, get the right encoded header value.

deprecate mixed string/bytes response iterable
`Response.response` has been annotated as `Iterable[bytes] | Iterable[str]` for a long time now. However, for historic reasons (Python 2's mixed str/bytes type, presumably), it can actually be a mixed `Iterable[bytes | str]`, because `Response.iter_encoded` does an instance check for every yielded item. While passing an iterable of strings is useful (for example, a generator with `csv.writer`), there should be absolutely no reason to have strings and bytes in the iterator. We could make `Response.iter_encoded` _hugely_ more efficient by only checking the type of the first item, then assuming it for the rest.

`direct_passthrough` is currently documented as useful for files, or for if you know the response is all bytes. With this change, it should only really be necessary for files/`wsgi.file_wrapper`. An iterator that just yields from another iterator (in the case of bytes) should be essentially no overhead.

dev server doesn't close response iterable when client resets connection
If the client resets the connection while the dev server is sending a response, the response iterable's `close()` is never called. With `send_file` this leaves the file open, and you get `ResourceWarning: unclosed file` later. Under `pytest -W error` that fails an unrelated test. I see it in browser tests when a page closes while an asset is still downloading.

```python
import socket
import struct
import threading
import time

from werkzeug.serving import make_server


class Body:
    def __iter__(self):
        for _ in range(1000):
            yield b"x" * 65536

    def close(self):
        print("closed")


def app(environ, start_response):
    start_response("200 OK", [("Content-Type", "text/plain")])
    return Body()


server = make_server("127.0.0.1", 0, app)
threading.Thread(target=server.serve_forever, daemon=True).start()

sock = socket.create_connection(("127.0.0.1", server.port))
sock.sendall(b"GET / HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: localhost\r\n\r\n")
sock.recv(4096)
# close with RST instead of FIN
sock.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_LINGER, struct.pack("ii", 1, 0))
sock.close()
time.sleep(1)
server.shutdown()
```

Expected: `closed` is printed.

Actual: nothing is printed (10 of 10 runs).

Cause: `write()` fails with the reset, then the `finally` block in `run_wsgi` drains the socket before closing the iterable. The socket is readable because of the reset, so `self.rfile.read(10_000_000)` raises `ConnectionResetError`, which skips `selector.close()` and `application_iter.close()`.

https://github.com/pallets/werkzeug/blob/85dd69bda8f7591089ded638b67d57cf496676fb/src/werkzeug/serving.py#L343-L371

Catching `OSError` around that read and breaking out of the loop fixes it. I have that change with a test, and can open a PR against `stable` if that works for you.

Deprecate separate utility functions in favor of `Request` and `Response`
https://werkzeug.palletsprojects.com/en/stable/levels/#high-or-low suggests that you might want to choose to use the individual utility functions on an `environ` rather than using `Request`. But I'm not sure any of the reasons hold up.

`Request` is an extremely lightweight wrapper around `environ`. There's essentially no cost to constructing it, and then it offers a way better (and more complete) API than the various utility functions. Similarly for `Response`.

Most behavior has already been moved into the sans-io base class, to move towards supporting an ASGI implementation. The utilities that still exist are mostly wrappers around sans-io implementations, but those are all available through the `Request` properties anyway.

Behavior that is truly WSGI-specific (input handling) can either be kept as private helpers, or inlined into the `Request` properties.

This would probably cut down on a lot of #3281 as well, since most of that is for the WSGI utilities.

| utility | `Request` property, etc |
| --- | --- |
| `wsgi.get_current_url` | `url`, `base_url`, `root_url`, `host_url` |
| `wsgi.get_host` | `host` |
| `wsgi.get_content_length` | `content_length` |
| `wsgi.get_input_stream`, `LimitedStream` | `stream` |
| `wsgi.wrap_file`, `FileWrapper` | `send_file`, #3301; keep `wrap_file` it doesn't clearly belong to `Request` or `Response` |
| `wsgi._RangeWrapper` | already private, `Response.apply_range` #3291 |
| `wsgi.ClosingIterator` | use `Response` as a WSGI application callable, or use `Response.from_app`, but keep for rare cases where it's simpler than those |
| `utils.get_content_type` | set `Response.mimetype` |
| `utils.append_slash_redirect` | `Map` `strict_slashes` |
| `formparser.parse_form_data`, `FormDataParser` | `form`, `files` |
| `http.generate_etag` | `Response.add_etag` |
| `http.parse_age`, `dump_age` | already private, `Response.age` |
| `http.remove_hop_by_hop_headers`, `is_hop_by_hop_header` | first is unused, second is useful for the rare case of proxies, needs to be updated for RFC 9110 |
| `http.remove_entity_headers`, `is_entity_header` | `Response.get_wsgi_headers`, or the server handles it, needs to be updated for RFC 9110 |
| `http.parse_cookie`, `dump_cookie` | `Request.cookies`, `Response.set_cookie` |

is_normalized_name() rejects some names that canonicalize_name() leaves unchanged (leading/trailing hyphens)
Spotted by @henryiii while reviewing #1230.

`is_normalized_name(name)` is documented to return `True` iff the name is already canonical (`canonicalize_name(name) == name`, i.e. it roundtrips). That holds in the interior but breaks at the edges: `canonicalize_name` can emit names with leading/trailing hyphens (it lowercases and collapses `[-_.]+` to `-` without stripping edge hyphens), yet `is_normalized_name` rejects those.

Reproducer (packaging 26.0):

```python
from packaging.utils import canonicalize_name, is_normalized_name
n = canonicalize_name("_not_legal")   # -> "-not-legal"
print(canonicalize_name(n) == n)       # True  (already canonical / roundtrips)
print(is_normalized_name(n))           # False (contract says this should be True)
```

Same for `"a-"`, `"-a"`, `"-not-legal"`. An exhaustive `{a,1,-}`-style enumeration shows the divergence is exactly the leading/trailing-hyphen class (henryiii counted 895 such names in the #1230 review).

Root cause: `is_normalized_name` matches `[a-z0-9]+(?:-[a-z0-9]+)*` (PEP 503 valid-name shape — no leading/trailing hyphen), while `canonicalize_name` never strips edge hyphens, so it can produce strings the regex won't accept.

These aren't valid distribution names, so the practical impact is narrow, but the two functions disagree on their documented relationship. Resolution is a maintainer call — tighten `canonicalize_name` to strip edge hyphens, relax `is_normalized_name` to mirror `canonicalize_name`'s output, or document the edge in the "iff roundtrips" wording. Filing per @henryiii's note in #1230 to keep track.

CSV streaming (?_stream=on) on a SQL view loops forever, re-serving the same page
In 1.0a38, streaming a **view** as CSV with `?_stream=on` never terminates. The stream advances one page, then repeats that same page indefinitely until `max_csv_mb` truncates the response. Streaming a **table** works correctly. The issue doesn't seem to exist in 0.65.3, the latest 0.x release.

## Context

We have recently deployed a new database served by Datasette 1.0a38, which exposes several SQL views as the public query surface. We first implemented CSV downloads with `?_size=max`, but some initial testing of the CSV streaming functionality suggested that a switch to `?_stream=on` could lighten the load on the server. That is when we found the conflict with views: streaming works on a table, but a single `?_stream=on` request against a view pins CPU generating hundreds of MB of duplicated rows on a small database and never completes.

## What happens

If you stream a 500-row view with `?_stream=on`, the response never ends. In a ~15s capture it produced roughly 1.19M data rows, but only **200 distinct primary-key values**. Datasette appears to emit page 1 (rows 1–100) once, then emit page 2 (rows 101–200) on every subsequent iteration, never advancing past it. Streaming the same data as a **table** returns all 500 rows exactly once.

The problem is likely due to the fact that tables and views paginate differently: tables paginate by keyset, views paginate by `OFFSET`, and only the `OFFSET` path is broken.

## Diagnosis and fix (proposed by Claude Opus after autonomous testing and debugging)

The streaming loop threads the pagination cursor back into `table_view_data` as a `_next` keyword argument. That argument is honored once, then discarded before the next cursor is computed.

In `datasette/views/table.py`, the kwarg is honored to build the page's `OFFSET`:

```python
# datasette/views/table.py:2054
_next = _next or request.args.get("_next")
```

Later in the same function, just before the next-page token is computed, `_next` is re-read from the request arguments and the honored kwarg is overwritten:

```python
# datasette/views/table.py:2229
_next = request.args.get("_next")
```

During a stream `_next` is never present in the request arguments. `stream_csv` passes it only as a kwarg, and rejects it as a query argument outright:

```python
# datasette/views/base.py:198
if request.args.get("_next"):
    raise BadRequest("_next not allowed for CSV streaming")
```

So line 2229 always sets `_next = None` in the streaming case. The next-token computation for a view then reads that `None`:

```python
# datasette/views/table.py:2425
if is_view:
    next_value = int(_next or 0) + page_size   # int(None or 0) + page_size == page_size, every time
else:
    next_value = path_from_row_pks(rows[-2], pks, use_rowid)  # derived from the last row, unaffected
```

`next_value` is therefore pinned at `page_size` for every iteration, so the loop re-requests `OFFSET page_size` forever. The table branch derives its token from the last row of the page, so it advances correctly and never loops.

Between line 2054 and line 2229 there is no other assignment to `_next`, so line 2229 is a redundant re-read that only discards the honored value. Removing it (or making it non-clobbering, `_next = _next or request.args.get("_next")`) lets the view branch see the real offset. With that single line changed, the same 500-row view streams 500 rows / 500 distinct keys and terminates.

## Not present in the 0.x line

0.65.3 has the equivalent honor line but no clobbering re-read before the token computation:

- `datasette/views/table.py:354` (0.65.3) honors `_next = _next or request.args.get("_next")`
- `datasette/views/table.py:627` (0.65.3) computes `next_value = int(_next or 0) + page_size` from the still-honored value

The clobbering re-read was introduced when the table view was reworked from the class-based `RowTableShared.data` method into the functional `table_view_data`. `main` still carries it at `table.py:2229`.

## Reproduction

```python
import sqlite3
con = sqlite3.connect("repro.db")
con.execute("CREATE TABLE base (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, val INTEGER)")
con.executemany(
    "INSERT INTO base (id, name, val) VALUES (?, ?, ?)",
    [(i, f"row-{i}", i * 7 % 1000) for i in range(1, 501)],
)
con.execute("CREATE VIEW v_base AS SELECT id, name, val FROM base")
con.commit()
con.close()
```

```
datasette repro.db --setting max_returned_rows 1000000
```

- `curl 'http://localhost:8001/repro/base.csv?_stream=on'` returns 500 rows, 500 distinct ids. Correct.
- `curl 'http://localhost:8001/repro/v_base.csv?_stream=on'` never completes; the body is rows 1–200 repeated until `max_csv_mb` cuts it off.

Count distinct ids in the captured body to see the loop:

```
curl -s --max-time 15 'http://localhost:8001/repro/v_base.csv?_stream=on' \
  | tail -n +2 | cut -d, -f1 | sort -u | wc -l   # -> 200, not 500
```

## Impact

- Any `?_stream=on` request against a view generates duplicated rows up to `max_csv_mb`, which is wasted CPU and memory per request and a broken export.
- Tables are unaffected.
- The fix is confined to the view (`OFFSET`) pagination path; the table (keyset) path already ignores the clobbered value, so removing the redundant re-read does not change table behavior.

## Versions

```
datasette: 1.0a38
sqlite:    3.53.1
python:    3.13
```

The streaming loop threads the pagination cursor back into `table_view_data` as a `_next` keyword argument. That argument is honored once, then discarded before the next cursor is computed.

In `datasette/views/table.py`, the kwarg is honored to build the page's `OFFSET`:

```python
# datasette/views/table.py:2054
_next = _next or request.args.get("_next")
```

Later in the same function, just before the next-page token is computed, `_next` is re-read from the request arguments and the honored kwarg is overwritten:

```python
# datasette/views/table.py:2229
_next = request.args.get("_next")
```

During a stream `_next` is never present in the request arguments. `stream_csv` passes it only as a kwarg, and rejects it as a query argument outright:

```python
# datasette/views/base.py:198
if request.args.get("_next"):
    raise BadRequest("_next not allowed for CSV streaming")
```

So line 2229 always sets `_next = None` in the streaming case. The next-token computation for a view then reads that `None`:

```python
# datasette/views/table.py:2425
if is_view:
    next_value = int(_next or 0) + page_size   # int(None or 0) + page_size == page_size, every time
else:
    next_value = path_from_row_pks(rows[-2], pks, use_rowid)  # derived from the last row, unaffected
```

`next_value` is therefore pinned at `page_size` for every iteration, so the loop re-requests `OFFSET page_size` forever. The table branch derives its token from the last row of the page, so it advances correctly and never loops.

Between line 2054 and line 2229 there is no other assignment to `_next`, so line 2229 is a redundant re-read that only discards the honored value. Removing it (or making it non-clobbering, `_next = _next or request.args.get("_next")`) lets the view branch see the real offset. With that single line changed, the same 500-row view streams 500 rows / 500 distinct keys and terminates.

## Not present in the 0.x line

0.65.3 has the equivalent honor line but no clobbering re-read before the token computation:

- `datasette/views/table.py:354` (0.65.3) honors `_next = _next or request.args.get("_next")`
- `datasette/views/table.py:627` (0.65.3) computes `next_value = int(_next or 0) + page_size` from the still-honored value

The clobbering re-read was introduced when the table view was reworked from the class-based `RowTableShared.data` method into the functional `table_view_data`. `main` still carries it at `table.py:2229`.

```python
con = sqlite3.connect("repro.db")
con.execute("CREATE TABLE base (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, val INTEGER)")
con.executemany(
    "INSERT INTO base (id, name, val) VALUES (?, ?, ?)",
    [(i, f"row-{i}", i * 7 % 1000) for i in range(1, 501)],
)
con.execute("CREATE VIEW v_base AS SELECT id, name, val FROM base")
con.commit()
con.close()
```

```
datasette repro.db --setting max_returned_rows 1000000
```

- `curl 'http://localhost:8001/repro/base.csv?_stream=on'` returns 500 rows, 500 distinct ids. Correct.
- `curl 'http://localhost:8001/repro/v_base.csv?_stream=on'` never completes; the body is rows 1–200 repeated until `max_csv_mb` cuts it off.

Count distinct ids in the captured body to see the loop:

```

  | tail -n +2 | cut -d, -f1 | sort -u | wc -l   # -> 200, not 500
```

## Impact

- Any `?_stream=on` request against a view generates duplicated rows up to `max_csv_mb`, which is wasted CPU and memory per request and a broken export.
- Tables are unaffected.
- The fix is confined to the view (`OFFSET`) pagination path; the table (keyset) path already ignores the clobbered value, so removing the redundant re-read does not change table behavior.

execute_write_fn(block=False) raises TypeError when num_sql_threads is 0
With `num_sql_threads` set to `0`, `await db.execute_write_fn(fn, block=False)` raises `TypeError: cannot unpack non-iterable NoneType object` instead of returning a UUID.

The docs describe `block=False` as fire-and-forget returning a task id:

> If you specify `block=False` the method becomes fire-and-forget [...] A UUID representing the queued task will be returned.

## Cause

In `datasette/database.py`, `execute_write_fn` takes a non-threaded branch when there is no executor, so `result` is whatever `fn` returned:

```python
if self.ds.executor is None:
    # non-threaded mode
    ...
    result = fn(self._write_connection)
else:
    result = await self._send_to_write_thread(fn, block=block, transaction=transaction)
```

The `block=False` path then unpacks `result` unconditionally:

```python
else:
    # For non-blocking writes, spawn a background task ...
    task_id, reply_future = result
```

Only `_send_to_write_thread` returns the `(task_id, reply_future)` pair. In the non-threaded branch `result` is the function's return value, which for an ordinary write function is `None`.

## Reproduction

Against `e889403d3bbe143854262682161c98a57bdb6594`:

```python
import asyncio
from datasette.app import Datasette

async def main():
    ds = Datasette(memory=True, settings={"num_sql_threads": 0})
    await ds.invoke_startup()
    db = ds.add_memory_database("repro")

    def make_table(conn):
        conn.execute("CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS t (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, v TEXT)")

    await db.execute_write_fn(make_table, block=True)   # fine

    def w(conn):
        conn.execute("INSERT INTO t (v) VALUES ('a')")  # returns None

    await db.execute_write_fn(w, block=False)           # TypeError

asyncio.run(main())
```

```
TypeError: cannot unpack non-iterable NoneType object
```

`block=True` works in the same configuration, and both work with the default `num_sql_threads`.

## Scope, and what I am not claiming

- This only affects `num_sql_threads = 0`. The default configuration is unaffected.
- I have not found an in-core caller that hits this, so I am not claiming a user-facing break in shipped Datasette. It is reachable from the documented plugin API.
- I have not tested this under Pyodide itself, only with the setting that selects the same branch.
- No security or data-loss impact is claimed. The write is applied before the unpack raises, so the failure is in the return path, not the write.

## Possible fix

Return a task id in the non-threaded branch too, so the documented contract holds, or skip the unpack when there is no executor. I did not want to guess which shape you would prefer, and I am happy to send a PR with tests once you say which.

execute_write_fn(block=False) returns the same task_id for every write
`_send_to_write_thread()` derives the task id from a constant, so every non-blocking write in every database in every process returns the same UUID.

https://github.com/simonw/datasette/blob/e889403d3bbe143854262682161c98a57bdb6594/datasette/database.py#L428

```python
task_id = uuid.uuid5(uuid.NAMESPACE_DNS, "datasette.io")
```

`uuid5` is deterministic: same namespace plus same name gives the same UUID forever. The value is always:

```
3f143baa-4e3d-5842-a36f-4fa2f683b72f
```

The docs describe this return value as identifying the specific queued task:

> A UUID representing the queued task will be returned.

A constant cannot represent a particular task, so a caller cannot use it to tell two queued writes apart.

## Reproduction

Against `e889403d3bbe143854262682161c98a57bdb6594`:

```python
import asyncio
from datasette.app import Datasette

async def main():
    ds = Datasette([], memory=True)
    await ds.invoke_startup()
    db = ds.add_memory_database("m")
    await db.execute_write("create table t (id integer primary key, v text)")

    def w(conn):
        conn.execute("insert into t (v) values ('a')")

    ids = [await db.execute_write_fn(w, block=False) for _ in range(5)]
    print(len(set(ids)), "distinct id(s) from 5 writes")
    print(ids[0])

asyncio.run(main())
```

```
1 distinct id(s) from 5 writes
3f143baa-4e3d-5842-a36f-4fa2f683b72f
```

The existing test `test_execute_write_fn_block_false` asserts only `isinstance(task_id, uuid.UUID)`, which a constant satisfies, so this is not currently caught.

## History

Introduced in 4284c74bc133ab494bf4b6dcd4a20b97b05ebb83 (`db.execute_isolated_fn()` method, #2220, 2023-12-19), and present in releases from `1.0a10` onward. It is long-standing rather than a recent regression.

## Scope, and what I am not claiming

- The writes themselves are correct. Every queued function runs, in order, and its result is delivered on the right future. `WriteTask.task_id` is not used for dispatch, so nothing is misrouted.
- I have not found an in-core consumer of the returned id, so I am not claiming a user-facing break in shipped Datasette. The impact is on the documented plugin API.
- No security or data-loss impact is claimed.

## Fix

`uuid.uuid4()` restores the documented contract. Happy to send a PR with a regression test that asserts two calls return different ids, alongside the fix for #2859 which is in the same method.
